sources.what: Tyndale, The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528): the passage defending Scripture in the mother tongue
sources.note: No verified online text yet. Candidates: Parker Society, Doctrinal Treatises (ed. Henry Walter, 1848) on archive.org (identifier not found); the EEBO-TCP transcription (Oxford Text Archive A18673, blocked to us). IMPORTANT: the ploughboy vow is NOT in the Obedience: it is Foxe's report of Tyndale's words to a learned man ('I will cause a boy that driveth the plough shall know more of the Scripture than thou dost'). Take it from Foxe (Gutenberg #22400, check it is in the abridgement).

art.title: Saint Mark
art.why: No medieval manuscript Bible in the NGA. An evangelist reading a Latin book with quill and inkpot: the Gospel in Latin, the only Bible the West had before Wycliffe.

art.title: Landscape with Peasants
art.why: No Tyndale. Country children and an old woman by the fields: the ploughboy's world, the reader Tyndale wrote for.

art.title: The Singing Party
art.why: Men and a boy singing from one book: psalms in English as something sung together.

art.title: Hampton Court Green
art.why: The place where James I agreed to the new translation in 1604. FLAG: a nineteenth-century scene, not the conference; use only with that said plainly, or null.

art.title: Woman Reading in the Studio
art.why: A reader with an open book: the KJV's life in private reading.

art.title: The Adoration of the Shepherds
art.why: No annunciation to the shepherds is free; this is the next moment of the same passage (Luke 2:15–16), at night.
